Eigenvalues and zero eigenvalues
Let \(A\) be an \(n\times n\) real matrix. Which statements are true
RightAnswers

column3: If \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\) then \(A\) is non invertible
If \(A\) is non invertible then \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\)
If \(A\) has a zero row then \(0\) must be an eigenvalue of \(A\)
If \(A\) has a zero eigenvalue then \(\det(A)=0\)

column2: Think about how the determinant relates to eigenvalues
Zero determinant and zero eigenvalue are tightly related

Maximum of xT A x for unit x
Let \(A\) be symmetric with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\). What is true about \(\max_{\|x\|=1} x^TAx\)
RightAnswers

column3: The maximum equals \(\lambda_1\)
It is attained exactly at eigenvectors corresponding to \(\lambda_1\)
It depends on the choice of basis
For all unit \(x\) we have \(x^TAx\le \lambda_1\)

Let \(A\) be symmetric with eigenpairs \((\lambda_i
column3: v_i)\). Which statements are true about \(A^k\) for an integer \(k\ge 1\)

column2: RightAnswers

column3: The eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda_i^k\)
Every eigenvector of \(A\) is an eigenvector of \(A^k\)
The eigenvalue multiplicities are always preserved for all integers \(k\ge 1\)
The matrix \(A^k\) is diagonalizable if and only if \(A\) is diagonalizable

column2: Use the spectral decomposition of \(A\) and raise it to the power \(k\)
Diagonalization makes the effect of powers on eigenvalues and eigenvectors transparent

Relating eigenvectors of A^T A and A A^T
Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) real matrix. Suppose \(\sigma^2>0\) is a nonzero eigenvalue of both \(A^TA\) and \(AA^T\). Which statements are true
RightAnswers

column3: If \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(A^TA\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2\) then \(Av\) is an eigenvector of \(AA^T\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2\)
If \(u\) is an eigenvector of \(AA^T\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2\) then \(A^Tu\) is an eigenvector of \(A^TA\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2\)
The nonzero eigenvalues of \(A^TA\) and \(AA^T\) always coincide and are counted with multiplicity
If \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(A^TA\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2>0\) then \(Av\neq 0\) and if \(u\) is an eigenvector of \(AA^T\) with eigenvalue \(\sigma^2>0\) then \(A^Tu\neq 0\)

column2: Think about the singular value decomposition and how it connects these two matrices
Nonzero eigenvalues of \(A^TA\) and \(AA^T\) correspond to squared singular values and share linked eigenvectors

Spectral decomposition of a symmetric matrix
Let \(A\) be a real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix with spectral decomposition \(A = V\Lambda V^T\). Which statements are true
RightAnswers

column3: Columns of \(V\) can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
The diagonal entries of \(\Lambda\) are eigenvalues of \(A\) listed with algebraic multiplicity
If all eigenvalues of \(A\) are distinct then the decomposition is unique up to signs of the eigenvectors
For a symmetric matrix \(A\) it may happen that there is no orthogonal \(V\) and diagonal \(\Lambda\) such that \(A = V\Lambda V^T\)

column2: Recall the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices
The spectral theorem guarantees an orthogonal eigenbasis and a decomposition \(A = V\Lambda V^T\)
